title: Selective delegation: Rapid drafting proves little reliability
desc: Treats adoption, self-service and task suitability separately while emphasizing hands-on learning and disputed technical literacy needs.

kps.k: The cluster frames AI adoption as selective delegation of tasks, not wholesale replacement of lawyers.
kps.d: The central proposition is that lawyers should experiment with drafting, summarisation, text manipulation and routine queries while retaining responsibility for interpretation and strategic advice. Miller’s 2017 account anticipates this division of labour for legal AI generally; his later generative-AI guidance develops it into supervised practice. Cooke similarly reserves business-critical, strategy-dependent advice for humans, at least for now. Expected gains in capacity, higher-value work and reduced burnout remain forecasts rather than demonstrated outcomes.

qs.q: Rather, embrace it as, ultimately, it will allow you to do thing things lawyers love to do: thinking, analyzing, and counseling, while leaving the “grunt” work to the computer.
qs.a: Ten Things: Artificial Intelligence — What Every Legal Department Really Needs to Know · In-house counsel · 2017

qs.q: ChatGPT/generative AI will be another tool you can use to streamline tasks and reduce the amount of mundane work you must deal with (for example [a chatbot to answer frequently asked questions](https://craftycounsel.co.uk/real-life-stories-of-generative-ai-for-in-house-legal-with-andy-cooke/)) and, instead, free you to work on complex, high-value projects where you truly show your value.
qs.a: Ten Things: ChatGPT and Generative AI (What In-House Counsel Need to Know) · In-house counsel · 2023

kps.k: Concrete experiments establish adoption and rapid text production, but not reliable legal performance or net productivity gains.
kps.d: Miller reports usable NDA and indemnity drafts produced in seconds, without reproducing them. The author of The Implications of ChatGPT for Legal Services and Society reports drafting most of a paper through prompts in about an hour in December 2022, largely without editing. Green describes Gunderson Dettmer’s August 2023 ChatGD launch, while Cooke describes a chatbot trial whose workflow effects remained to be assessed. These accounts lack systematic comparative outcomes. Cooke’s assertions of over 70% question-answering accuracy for GPT-3.5 and over 90% for GPT-4 have no supplied test method and are not TravelPerk trial results. Product descriptions in the Law Society primer likewise do not establish effectiveness.

qs.q: While I will not set these out in this post, while I was playing with it, I next asked it to “Prepare a simple mutual non-disclosure agreement for a business using Texas law and exclusion jurisdiction in Texas” and got back a usable first draft.
qs.a: Ten Things: ChatGPT and Generative AI (What In-House Counsel Need to Know) · In-house counsel · 2023

qs.q: In fact, within a few months of ChatGPT’s      release, law firms and legal tech companies are already announcing new      ways of using generative AI tools.2           To demonstrate the potential implications of AI, both for legal      services and society, I drafted most of this paper in about an hour      through prompts within ChatGPT on December 5, 2022.

kps.k: Self-service offers a distinct scaling mechanism, but moves the delegation question beyond lawyer-supervised drafting.
kps.d: Cooke argues that additional headcount cannot meet expectations for immediate answers to repetitive internal questions. His proposed mechanism uses existing policy documents to reduce the manual decision-tree work required by conventional chatbots. Miller also recommends internal FAQs and document assembly. Separately, the 2025 access-to-justice report describes public-facing intake and legal information tools and asks the legal services community to define acceptable delegation around both represented clients and people turned away. Enterprise responsiveness and unmet civil legal need are different objectives; neither account establishes that direct AI responses meet the necessary quality standard.

qs.q: You cannot meet this standard by adding more people to the Legal function.
qs.a: Real life stories of generative AI for in-house legal: Andy Cooke · In-house counsel · 2023

qs.q: - Find a way to make the department’s AI tools available to the business as part of a self-help initiative, e.g., FAQ chatbot or document assembly tool on your intranet site.
qs.a: Ten Things: ChatGPT and Generative AI (What In-House Counsel Need to Know) · In-house counsel · 2023

kps.k: The sources differ over task suitability and future capability, rather than simply dividing into adoption advocates and opponents.
kps.d: ChatGD’s 2023 training favoured text manipulation and judged search-engine replacement premature. The Fifth Circuit proposal commentary describes research opportunities conditional on access to legal databases and reports suggestions for testing appellate arguments. Generative Artificial Intelligence and the Practice of Law predicts substantial gains in some research and writing but little help with highly fact-specific reasoning, whereas Miller expects legal capabilities eventually to catch up with the hype. These are differing expectations and tool contexts, not comparative tests. Miller’s May 2023 cutoff and connectivity limitations should not be generalised to later systems.

qs.q: We also shared ideal use cases for GenAI (e.g., text manipulation) and areas where we thought the technology was not well suited for use without further advancements (e.g., search engine replacement).

kps.k: Hands-on learning and shared workflows underpin adoption, but sources disagree about how much technical understanding users need.
kps.d: Miller and the ethics podcast recommend low-risk experimentation and learning how context, question framing and tool choice affect outputs. The AI-Empowered Counsel recommends curated, version-controlled prompt libraries for recurring departmental tasks. Green describes mandatory, role-specific training and collective use-case discovery before ChatGD access. A substantive difference concerns technical literacy: Miller’s 2025 advice treats underlying mechanics as largely irrelevant to ordinary users, while ChatGD training explicitly taught LLM and retrieval-augmented generation mechanics. Claims that shared prompts improve reliability remain guidance, not measured results; the Law Society presents clearer prompting more narrowly as improving alignment with user intentions.

qs.q: - Start small and with free products and low-risk tasks (understanding the risks) and get your feet wet.
qs.a: Ten Things: ChatGPT and Generative AI (What In-House Counsel Need to Know) · In-house counsel · 2023

qs.q: This is a curated, version-controlled repository of best-in-class prompts for your department’s most common tasks.
qs.a: The AI-Empowered Counsel: A Practical Framework for In-house Legal Teams · In-house counsel · 2025

kps.k: Verification and tool-specific data safeguards qualify the promise of easy productivity gains.
kps.d: Miller’s junior-assistant analogy requires context, iteration and human checking; his personal experience of limited fabrication is not an error-rate estimate. The Law Society warns that generated output cannot establish its own accuracy. The ethics checklist adds vendor due diligence, bias review, records of inputs and errors, and liability planning. Miller recommends restricting sensitive inputs and carefully anonymising documents, particularly outside bespoke enterprise environments, while acknowledging that privacy controls only reduce risk. In practice, the adoption case must account for preparation, training, sanitisation and verification time rather than equating generation speed with time saved.

qs.q: **This means that generative AI cannot autonomously validate or audit the accuracy of its results.
qs.a: Generative AI: the essentials · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: They should be prepared to do that diligence by having a list of questions or factors to address, whether these are questions relating to confidentiality, data privacy and security, transparency, potential bias or any of the topics listed above.
qs.a: Ethics of Artificial Intelligence for the Legal Practitioner · Regulators & courts · 2024

kps.k: Governance must address how AI contributes to legal work, not merely whether generated prose appears in the final document.
kps.d: Miller recommends departmental and company-wide policies and legal participation in corporate adoption decisions. The ethics article extends governance to client expectations, input and output rights, insurance and service quality. Miller interprets ABA Model Rule 1.4 as requiring client notification but directs lawyers to applicable local rules; this is not a universal disclosure rule. Commentary on the Fifth Circuit’s proposed certification reads drafting-process disclosure as encompassing analytical assistance even when generated wording is excluded. That interpretation concerns a proposal the court did not adopt in June 2024, not an operative requirement. Together, these contributions place process accountability alongside output checking.

vlens.an: The curated in-house counsel and legal-operations sources collectively accept the proposition’s core: AI should be delegated bounded, routine tasks—such as drafting, summarisation, information synthesis and repetitive internal queries—while lawyers retain responsibility for verification, interpretation and strategy. They build materially on that proposition by supplying an operating model for adoption: begin with low-risk use cases, treat the system like a supervised junior assistant, provide context and iterate, protect confidential data, and institutionalise recurring work through shared prompt libraries and departmental governance. Their common rationale is capacity: rapid first drafts and self-service may reduce repetitive work and let lawyers concentrate on higher-value advice. Material variation concerns the mechanism and degree of confidence. Cooke prioritises direct internal self-service and anticipates scalability, but reports a trial whose workflow effects were still to be assessed. Miller’s 2017 account is primarily predictive; his later guidance is more cautious and operational, stressing verification, preparation costs, privacy and professional accountability. The AI-Empowered Counsel advances a department-wide prompting system but asserts accurate, reliable outputs without supplying measured validation. Thus, these sources strengthen the selective-delegation model without establishing that generation speed translates into reliable legal performance or net productivity gains; their views should not be treated as representative of all in-house professionals.

qs.q: To do this at an enterprise level, you must move beyond individual ad-hoc efforts and build a centralized prompt library.
qs.a: The AI-Empowered Counsel: A Practical Framework for In-house Legal Teams · In-house counsel · 2025

vlens.an: The traditional-law-firm voice represented here accepts the cluster’s principal proposition of selective delegation and materially develops its implementation model. Green’s account treats generative AI as a supervised, evolving experiment rather than a substitute for lawyers: access depended on training, users collectively identified promising workflows, and the firm distinguished suitable text-manipulation tasks from uses it considered premature, notably search-engine replacement. This adds concrete organisational practices—role-specific upskilling, technical and ethical instruction, collaborative use-case discovery, and explicit task boundaries—to the cluster’s broader case for hands-on learning. The principal limitation is evidential: the account demonstrates deployment and an adoption process, but reports no systematic results on legal reliability, verification burden, or net productivity. Because this professional voice contains only one curated source, there is no meaningful source-to-source variation to assess and no inference about the prevalence of this view among traditional law firms should be drawn. Within the account, the main tension is between active experimentation and caution about capability limits, but that caution reinforces rather than contradicts selective delegation.

qs.q: We framed the rollout of ChatGD as a collaborative experiment designed to help everyone move up the learning curve and to crowdsource the most promising use cases and methods for getting the best results out of GenAI-powered tools.
qs.a: ChatGD: Learnings (So Far) from our Legal GenAI Experiment · Law firms · 2023

qs.q: We also shared ideal use cases for GenAI (e.g., text manipulation) and areas where we thought the technology was not well suited for use without further advancements (e.g., search engine replacement).
qs.a: ChatGD: Learnings (So Far) from our Legal GenAI Experiment · Law firms · 2023

vlens.an: Across this curated set, regulators, courts and professional bodies accept the cluster’s core proposition that generative AI should be used through selective delegation rather than treated as a wholesale substitute for lawyers. They share three principal reasons: rapid generation and product adoption do not establish reliable legal performance; generative AI cannot independently validate its outputs; and lawyers remain responsible for verification, confidentiality, client interests and professional obligations. Collectively, the sources materially extend the proposition by specifying governance mechanisms around task-level use: tool-specific due diligence, fact-checking, recordkeeping, liability planning, client discussions and, in the Fifth Circuit proposal commentary, disclosure based on AI’s contribution to the drafting process even where generated prose is absent from the filing. There is material variation in emphasis. The ethics guidance supplies the most operational safeguards and treats efficiency and reduced burnout as predicted benefits. The Law Society primer is more cautious and educational, separating adoption aims and product descriptions from demonstrated effectiveness. The Fifth Circuit commentary advances a broad process-based disclosure interpretation, but it concerns a proposal the court ultimately did not adopt. The access-to-justice contribution shifts the focus toward collectively chosen delegation boundaries for represented and unserved clients and is comparatively optimistic that most ethical and privacy issues can be managed. None of these sources supplies systematic evidence of net productivity or reliable direct-to-public legal service.

vlens.an: The curated academia-and-research sources support the proposition’s distinction between selective use and reliable legal performance. Their common position is that generative AI can assist particular research, writing and drafting tasks, but capability varies by task and rapid production does not itself establish accuracy, quality or net productivity. They also favour informed experimentation rather than unsupervised reliance. Material variation lies in emphasis: one source gives practical advice on hands-on learning, prompting, tool choice, organisational rules and confidentiality; another predicts substantial efficiency gains for some tasks while expecting little help with highly fact- and case-specific reasoning; and the AI-drafted-paper experiment demonstrates production speed and breadth without validating legal reliability. These contributions are primarily practical guidance, forecasts and demonstrations rather than systematic comparative evidence.

qs.q: It argues that for some legal research and writing tasks, generative AI will lead to considerable efficiency improvements.
qs.a: Generative Artificial Intelligence and the Practice of Law: Impact, Opportunities, and Risks · Academia · 2024

qs.q: It also argues that there are aspects of legal writing—including reasoning and performing highly fact- and case-specific detailed analysis— where generative AI will offer little help.
qs.a: Generative Artificial Intelligence and the Practice of Law: Impact, Opportunities, and Risks · Academia · 2024

elens.an: The 2017 source supports the cluster’s principal proposition by presenting legal AI as selective task delegation rather than wholesale lawyer replacement. Miller assigns information-sifting and routine work to AI while reserving thinking, analysis and counseling for lawyers. His principal reason is functional division of labour: automation should free in-house counsel to focus on higher-value analytical and advisory work. There is material variation within the argument between a strong prediction that AI will become an indispensable, ubiquitous assistant and a narrower account of its role as a task-focused research assistant. The source does not provide measured evidence of reliability, legal performance or net productivity gains, nor does the supplied evidence develop the cluster’s later emphasis on verification and safeguards. Its support is therefore conceptual and predictive rather than empirical. Because the period evidence contains one curated source, it cannot establish how prevalent this position was among contemporary commentators.

qs.q: Put another way, “a research assistant” who can sift through the dreck and tell you what it found.

qs.q: Rather, embrace it as, ultimately, it will allow you to do thing things lawyers love to do: thinking, analyzing, and counseling, while leaving the “grunt” work to the computer.

elens.an: The curated 2023–2024 sources collectively accept the cluster’s principal proposition that generative AI is best used through selective, supervised delegation rather than wholesale lawyer replacement, and they materially develop its practical implementation. Common reasoning distinguishes routine or text-centred tasks—drafting first versions, summarisation, text manipulation, document comparison and repetitive internal queries—from strategic, interpretive and highly fact-specific legal work that remains lawyer-led. The sources also consistently separate impressive generation speed and adoption activity from demonstrated reliability or net productivity: reported experiments show usable drafts, rapid paper production, chatbot trials and internal deployment, but generally lack systematic comparisons, verified accuracy measures or accounting for training, preparation and verification time. Their material extension is an operational governance model built around low-risk experimentation, human verification, confidentiality and vendor due diligence, role-specific training, recordkeeping, client expectations and process-based accountability. Internal variation concerns where task boundaries should fall and what adoption requires. Cooke is comparatively optimistic about self-service for routine in-house demand, while reserving business-critical strategic advice for humans. The legal-practice article expects gains in some research and writing but little help with detailed reasoning. ChatGD treats text manipulation as suitable but search replacement as premature, whereas the Fifth Circuit commentary identifies database-connected research and argument testing as potential uses. Sources also differ between informal experimentation and structured institutional rollout, and between teaching underlying LLM/RAG mechanics and focusing primarily on practical prompting. Forecasts of greater capacity, broader service access and reduced burnout remain prospective rather than established findings.

qs.q: To take the latter example, an internal customer wanting to understand the intricacies of a single specific business critical contract and how this relates to our corporate strategy will probably want to speak with a lawyer and, indeed, is probably better served by a human.
qs.a: Real life stories of generative AI for in-house legal: Andy Cooke · In-house counsel · 2023

elens.an: The 2025 sources collectively accept the cluster’s principal proposition that legal AI should be adopted through selective, supervised delegation rather than treated as a substitute for lawyers, and they materially develop it into an operating model for broader organisational use. Their common reasoning is that AI is useful for bounded synthesis, drafting and routine work, while lawyers retain responsibility for strategic interpretation and verification. They also distinguish rapid output from demonstrated reliability or net productivity: the Law Society stresses that systems cannot validate their own results, Miller treats AI as a junior assistant whose work requires context, iteration and checking, and the in-house framework’s performance claims remain asserted rather than measured. The principal extension is practical infrastructure for adoption at scale: confidentiality controls, cautious task selection, structured prompting and a centralised, version-controlled prompt library. Material variation remains. The Law Society is the most institutionally cautious and emphasises uncertain long-term outcomes and incompletely understood risks; Miller offers experience-based confidence that simple uses can yield value but discounts the need for most lawyers to understand technical mechanics; the in-house framework makes stronger, untested claims about accurate summaries and consistent outputs and places greater weight on standardised prompting. These curated sources therefore build on the proposition through concrete implementation guidance without establishing systematic reliability or productivity gains.

qs.q: **This means that generative AI cannot autonomously validate or audit the accuracy of its results.
qs.a: Generative AI: the essentials · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: To do this at an enterprise level, you must move beyond individual ad-hoc efforts and build a centralized prompt library.
qs.a: The AI-Empowered Counsel: A Practical Framework for In-house Legal Teams · In-house counsel · 2025

elens.an: The 2026 source accepts the cluster’s principal proposition that GenAI adoption should be understood as selective delegation rather than wholesale lawyer replacement. It materially develops that proposition by shifting the decision boundary toward a collective, client-centered access-to-justice inquiry: the relevant clients include both people receiving representation and those denied help because resources are insufficient. It also reinforces the cluster’s distinction between adoption and demonstrated reliability, noting expanding public-facing use while leaving the quality of AI-provided legal information unresolved. Its principal internal qualification is comparatively optimistic: although it recognizes substantial ethical and privacy concerns, it argues that most are manageable through professional-conduct frameworks and precedents from earlier technologies. That confidence is an argument by analogy, not evidence that GenAI-specific risks or performance problems have been resolved.

qs.q: From my perspective, the fundamental question that needs to be addressed is what aspects of the practice of law will we be willing to delegate to GenAI.
